name: The Notch on the Post
summary: Ashwell's well-warden cuts a notch every Naming Day at how far the grey has come up the glass bed, and for the first time in a century this year's notch is above last year's. Walk the bed down to the Choir side and tell her what is coming up it.
notes: Ashwell's work (docs/ATLAS.md). Links Ashwell, the Wellspring, the Greyline Stones and Ash Watch: the grey is not coming on a front, it is coming up the glass bed behind a pilgrim walking water back.

stages.journal: Ada Welling walks the glass bed every Naming Day with a knotted cord until the grass stops being green, and cuts the notch at that many knots. For a hundred years the notches went down the post. This year's is above last year's. She has filled nine hundred and forty flasks at the Wellspring for pilgrims going south and not one has come back up the road, and this week one did: full, on the lip of the spring, with her own tally cut on its neck.

objectives.text: Walk down the glass bed to the Wellspring
Take up the flask left full on the lip of the spring

stages.journal: Nine hundred and twelve, the neck says: Hild Marrow, a dyer's widow from Merrowby, who walked south two summers ago and is written on the Order's Chapter Roll as gone on. The water in her flask is grey. Ada says the grey comes over the downs like flour on a south wind. It does not come up a riverbed like water, unless something is carrying it.

objectives.text: See where the grey begins, at the Greyline Stones
Ask at Ash Watch why its beacon was lit
Read the Ash Watch night-log

stages.journal: At the Greyline Stones the Wardens' new stone is set in front of last year's, not behind it: out on the open heath the ash has gone back. It is only on the glass bed that it comes on, a stride at a time, behind a woman in grey who walks up before dawn to fill a flask at the Wellspring and carry it back down to somebody. Ada Welling will want to hear that from somebody who has seen the log.

objectives.text: Tell Ada Welling what is coming up the bed, and what should be done about it

options.text: Put Hild Marrow down at the spring before she fills another flask.
Let her walk. She is carrying water to somebody.
Tell the Order at Pilgrim's Ash that one of theirs is walking back.

stages.journal: An hour before light, the log says, and she comes up careful of the glass's edges with a flask in both hands. Wait at the Wellspring for her.

objectives.text: Put down the grey walker at the Wellspring, before dawn

stages.journal: The Tolling Order keeps the Chapter Roll at Pilgrim's Ash, and a name on it is a name the Order has walked to the line and read aloud at Greywatch. Tell Cadwen Ash that one of the names she read is walking back up the glass bed with a flask.

objectives.text: Tell Cadwen Ash about Hild Marrow

stages.journal: Ada Welling cut this year's notch with the cord and the knife and washed the knife in the Lark Pool after, as she always does. She measured three times. She has put Hild Marrow's flask on the shelf in the well-house with the stopper in, and she says she will fill no flask she has not first cut a name on, because a flask with a name on it knows where it is going.

name: The Twelfth Sluice
summary: On nights the Toll hums, somebody opens the twelfth of Wynstead's sluices, the one with no name, and the water runs down the old lane to Gosford. Sit the night at the sluices, find out whose name the paddle had, and decide what Wynstead does with it.
notes: Wynstead's work. Links Wynstead, the Roll Stone and Merrowby (Pellam Ashcombe, who saw Gosford empty at twenty-two). Gosford is one of the four quiet villages (docs/ATLAS.md §13).

stages.journal: Wynstead floods its meadows in March through a chain of twelve oak sluices and drains them in May. Three nights this month the twelfth paddle has been lifted after dark, the one with no name on its post, and the water has run west across the low meadow onto the lane that went to Gosford: nine hearths, quiet in the eleven days the Toll hummed. The Toll is humming. Hal Wynstead has sat up two nights and seen nobody. Sit the third.

objectives.text: Sit the night at the sluices and meet whatever lifts the twelfth paddle

stages.journal: Two of them, grey as hedge-roots, came up the drowned lane at midnight and set their shoulders to the twelfth paddle as if they had done it every spring of their lives, and they had: they were working the water for Gosford's meadow. The post is bare. A sluice has a name the way a hearth does. Hal thinks somebody took this one off, and the Wardens cut names into stone when they take them off anything.

objectives.text: Look for the twelfth sluice's name at the Roll Stone
Ask Pellam Ashcombe, who saw Gosford empty, what the paddle was called

stages.journal: Under the four struck villages on the Roll Stone somebody has cut a fifth line in a Warden's square hand and struck it through: GOSFORD PADDLE. Pellam Ashcombe says the Wynsteads cut the name off the post the spring Gosford went, because a paddle that feeds a quiet meadow was thought unlucky, and a Warden cut it on the stone so that it would be struck somewhere and not simply lost. Gosford's meadow has been dry since. Gosford's dead have come to water it. Hal Wynstead has to decide what the twelfth paddle is now.

objectives.text: Tell Hal Wynstead what the twelfth paddle should be

options.text: Cut GOSFORD back on the post and let the paddle open on humming nights.
Nail the paddle down. The hay is Wynstead's and the lane is nobody's.
Tell the Wardens and let them put a watch on the lane.

stages.journal: The water is down off the low meadow and the lane is a lane again, a green one that goes to a green that goes to nothing. Hal Wynstead has written to his cousin Ellard in Merrowby about it, at length, which is how Hal says a thing is settled.

name: Thistle
summary: A ewe came back from Fallowfold's south pasture grey to the skin, and she still knows her name but will not go into the pond. The Vale keeps a thing by naming it; the shepherd wants to know who else has to say hers.
notes: Fallowfold's work. Links Fallowfold, the Ninth Waystone (whose bell-counts started again this spring in a hand the Order does not know) and, on one branch, Greywatch on the rim.

stages.journal: Thistle is four years old and has had twins twice. She came in grey to the skin under the fleece, eyes and all, and she comes to her name, but she will not go into the dew pond and will not come past the fold gate, and she stands at the south wall looking down at the heath as if somebody had called her. The south pasture runs down past the Old Sheepwash, whose spring has started moving again, a yard a day toward Fallowfold's gate, to the Ninth Waystone, where the pilgrims stop being Vale folk.

objectives.text: Look at the Old Sheepwash, whose spring is moving toward the fold
Walk the south pasture down to the Ninth Waystone

stages.journal: The Order scratches the year's bell-count into the Ninth Waystone, and the counts stop in 1024 and start again this spring. The new ones are not bells. They are cut shepherd-fashion, four strokes and a bar, the way Fallowfold counts a flock at the gate, and they are counting up, a few more every week. Somebody down in the grey is keeping a flock, and cutting its tally where a Vale shepherd would.

objectives.text: Tell Gil Fallow whose hand is on the waystone

stages.journal: Gil Fallow's father Aldo cut his tallies four strokes and a bar with the bar slanted, and walked south in the spring of 1024 because the grass was sweeter where it was poorer and he wanted to see how far that went. He is on the Chapter Roll as gone on. The counts on the waystone slant. Thistle stands at the south wall because she has heard him counting.

objectives.text: Decide with Gil Fallow who says Thistle's name

options.text: Say her name at the pond with the whole fold, loud, until she goes in.
Open the south gate. She is going to his count.
Ask the Order to read Aldo Fallow's name again at Greywatch, so his count ends.

stages.journal: The Order reads the names of the ones who walked down at three stones on the rim, because a name read carries further than a walk. Go to Greywatch and have Aldo Fallow read.

objectives.text: Have Aldo Fallow's name read at Greywatch

stages.journal: Gil Fallow has cut a notch of his own on the fold gate, four strokes and a bar with the bar slanted, which is not his way, and he has not said why and nobody at Fallowfold has asked.

name: The Top Bed
summary: Cressbourne's top watercress bed came up grey overnight. If it is the water the other beds go next; if it is the chalk it stops at the wall; if it is the Toll, nobody knows. Walk the Cressbourne up and down before the city tastes it.
notes: Cressbourne's work. Links Cressbourne, the Cress Bridge (somebody takes a coin a night, and the stream runs low) and the Limekilns, where the third kiln slakes with Cressbourne water and its lime has come out grey.

stages.journal: The top bed came up grey, as if the green had been drawn out of it with a thread; it tastes of nothing, which a cress should never do. The spring comes up under the top bed first. Upstream the carts to Tamwick cross the Cressbourne on three chalk slabs with a coin wedged in every joint, Tamwick's toll to the water, and somebody has been taking them, one a night, and the stream has started to run low.

objectives.text: Walk up the Cressbourne to the Cress Bridge
Catch whoever takes the coins, after dark
Find what the coin-taker was carrying

stages.journal: A Tollmere cutpurse, a long way from any purse, who had learned that the Vale leaves money lying in a bridge and nobody collects it. Thirty-one coins in a wet purse. The Cressbourne runs down past the beds to the Mere under the Lime Bridge, which the burners whitewash every spring with the first burn, and which came up grey under the whitewash this year; they slake their third kiln with it at the foot of the Whitecut.

objectives.text: Look at the Lime Bridge at the Cressbourne's mouth
See whether the grey has gone downstream as far as the Limekilns

stages.journal: The third kiln's lime has come out grey this spring, and the burners slake it with the Cressbourne. It is the water, then, and not the chalk, and whether it is the Toll too nobody can say, but the water was paid a coin a crossing for three hundred years and has been robbed of a month of them. Lin Cresswell will want to know, and she will want to say what is done with the purse.

objectives.text: Tell Lin Cresswell what the purse is for now

options.text: Wedge every coin back into the joints of the bridge.
Take the purse to the Guild's lost-coin box at the Stride's Foot.
Keep them. The water will not miss thirty-one coins.

stages.journal: Lin Cresswell has sent two carts down the coombe to the Stride this week as she always does, and she has sent the top bed's cress with them, grey, with a note to Tobin at the Toll's Lip telling him exactly what she thinks of fish.

name: Pens With No Gate
summary: The Wardens have ordered a mile of hurdles for pens on the grey border, with no gate, only a door barred from outside. Hazelcombe's master weaver will not weave a rod until somebody tells him what goes in them, and the Woodfolk have stopped selling him rods.
notes: Hazelcombe's work. Links Hazelcombe, the Wardens' Rest, the Rod Stacks and Hazelwick across the Wold's edge.

stages.journal: A mile of hurdles, to be carted to the border above the ash and set in pens: not folds, pens, with no gate, just a door you can bar from the outside. Tam Withy has woven for folds and pens and a Long Table dance floor once, and never for a pen with no gate. The Wardens told him the pens were for something that comes back grey. Ask them what.

objectives.text: Ask Sergeant Dole at the Wardens' Rest what the pens are for

stages.journal: Sergeant Dole says it plainly, the way he says everything: beasts are walking up out of the ash grey to the skin and going into the Vale's ponds, and the Rest wants them penned at the border before they do. Beasts, he says, and then after a while, and whatever else comes back. The Woodfolk sell Tam his rods at the Rod Stacks on the Wold's edge, and this season they have sold him none, and he would like to know who in the Wold is saying no.

objectives.text: Go to the Rod Stacks, where the Woodfolk sell the Vale its rods
Ask Aggie Coppice at Hazelwick why the Wold has stopped selling

stages.journal: Aggie Coppice cuts the Vale's rods, and she says the Wold does not sell hazel for a pen that nothing can walk out of. In the Wold a thing that has gone grey is let go, the way a named moss is let go when nobody remembers the name, and that is custom, and custom is not a thing she will argue about with a hurdle-maker. Tam Withy has the Wardens' order on his bench and no rods to weave it with, and a decision to make that is not a hurdle-maker's.

objectives.text: Tell Tam Withy how to weave the pens

options.text: Weave them as ordered. The Wardens keep the border; let them keep it.
Weave a gate into the south side, so what is penned can walk back down but not in.
Refuse the order. A pen nothing can leave is not a hurdle-maker's work.

stages.journal: Tam Withy has put one odd rod into every panel in the yard, as he always does, so that he can find his work. In the ones going to the border he has put two, and he says that is so he can find them faster, and he is not joking, and he is not smiling either.

name: One Short
summary: Every tally-stick in Bramcombe comes up one sheep short every morning, and no sheep is missing; the old tally in the wash-house beam, cut before the Toll fell, is one short too. Across the Vale, the Pinfold on the Eastway has one sheep more every morning than anybody put in it.
notes: Bramcombe's work. Links Bramcombe, the Pinfold by Merrowby and, on one branch, the Lambing Fold on Bram Down.

stages.journal: Every house in the combe keeps its own count and Pell Brambling keeps the combe's, and since spring they all agree and they are all one short, every morning, though he has counted the fold with his own mouth and there are exactly as many sheep as there should be. There is a tally in the wash-house beam that nobody can read, cut before the Toll fell, and it is one short too. Pell's sister Maud says it is the Toll humming. The Vale's strays are penned at the Pinfold on the Eastway.

objectives.text: Go to the Pinfold on the Eastway
Read the hayward's pound-book

stages.journal: One wether too many every morning since spring, a notch under and a notch over, which old Pellam told the hayward was the Bramcombe mark before the Toll fell, the one on the wash-house beam, and nobody has cut it in two hundred years. Nobody has paid the penny and nobody has rung the bell. The wether stands at the pound gate facing south-east, towards Bram Down.

objectives.text: Tell Pell Brambling whose mark the extra sheep carries

stages.journal: The combe's oldest tally counts a flock that was on Bram Down before the Toll fell, and it has been one short since spring, and one sheep with that flock's mark stands in a Vale pound every morning with nobody to ring the bell for it. Pell Brambling keeps the combe's count. It is his penny to pay, or not.

objectives.text: Decide with Pell Brambling what is done about the wether

options.text: Pay the penny, ring the bell, and walk him home to the combe.
Leave him in the pound. A sheep nobody owns is the hayward's business.
Drive him up to the Lambing Fold, to the ewe that belongs to nobody.

stages.journal: Rookdown's ewes lamb on Bram Down out of the wind off the Hush, and this spring a lamb was born there grey in the face to a ewe that belongs to nobody. Walk the wether up to the Lambing Fold.

objectives.text: Walk the wether up to the Lambing Fold

stages.journal: The sticks were laid side by side on the wash-house table at the end of the week, and Pell Brambling counted them twice and then counted the beam, and afterwards he went and sat in the sheep-wash with his boots on, which his sister says is what Bramblings do instead of saying something.

name: The Grey on the Green
summary: The grey patch on Rookdown's green has reached the well. Half the village wants to take the carts to Bramcombe and half says leaving is how a village goes quiet, and they have asked for somebody from outside to say which half is right. See what leaving looks like and what staying looks like, and say.
notes: Rookdown's work. Links Rookdown, the Last Field (the Southcotes left it), the Cliff Graves and the Brow Beacon.

stages.journal: The patch came up in the Quiet Villages years the size of a door and is the size of a threshing floor now; this week it touched the well. The water is still sweet. Tor Rookwright chalks the figure on the bell-post every Tollday and the village stands round and argues, which is the most talking Rookdown does. The Southcotes ploughed the Last Field to the Brow for three hundred years, and the year the grey reached the middle furrow they left the plough in it and walked to Rookdown.

objectives.text: See the Last Field, which the Southcotes left
Put down what works the grey furrows at night

stages.journal: Whatever the Southcotes left in their field has gone on ploughing it, grey furrow by grey furrow, with nobody to say whose field it is. Rookdown buries its drowned along the cliff facing the Hush so they will see it coming, and lights the Brow Beacon when it does. One headstone has turned inland in the night, and the beacon was lit twice this spring by a keeper who swears the Hush came up the cliff like a tide. Rookdown's sail-less mill on the Brow's back grinds on still nights with nobody in it, and the flour on its floor is grey.

objectives.text: Go up to Rook Mill, where the flour on the floor tastes of ash
Walk the Cliff Graves
Climb to the Brow Beacon

stages.journal: The turned headstone is a Rookwright's: Tor's grandmother's sister, drowned in 971, facing the village now instead of the water. The beacon-keeper says the Hush came up to the lip of the Brow and stood there, and went back down, like somebody who has come to a door and not knocked. Rookdown is waiting at the bell-post for somebody from outside.

objectives.text: Tell Rookdown which half is right

options.text: Stay. Say every name in the village at the bell-post each Tollday, louder than the grey.
Go to Bramcombe while the water is sweet. A village is its people, not its green.
Turn the headstone back to the Hush and let the drowned keep your watch.

stages.journal: Tor Rookwright chalked the week's figure on the bell-post under what you said, and the village read it and argued about it, which is what Rookdown does with anything it has decided.

name: The Warrener's Burrow
summary: Rookdown's warrener has not been home since the Long Table. His ferrets will not go down one burrow on the down, and every rabbit on Bram Down comes out of it; the Flint Pits' deepest shaft has started to ring, and Tallow Barrow's new wall has a door-shaped gap in it.
notes: Rookdown's second piece of work, once the grey on the green is settled. Links Rookdown, the Warrener's Camp, the Flint Pits and Tallow Barrow: the down is hollow between them.

stages.journal: The warrener keeps the down's rabbits in check and sells their skins in Tamwick, and has not been seen at home since the Long Table. His hut under the Thornmarch's gorse has his things in it and nobody. Tor Rookwright sent a boy up to feed the ferrets, and the boy came back and said the ferrets will not go down one burrow, and that every rabbit on the down comes up out of it, and then he would not go back.

objectives.text: Go up to the Warrener's Camp

stages.journal: The burrow the ferrets will not take runs west into the down, and the rabbits come out of it in a stream, not frightened, simply leaving. West along Bram Down the knappers of the Flint Pits say their deepest shaft has started to ring when it is struck, and that it started the week after the Long Table.

objectives.text: Ask the knappers at the Flint Pits about the ringing shaft

stages.journal: The knappers dropped a lamp down the deep shaft on a line and saw a chalk passage going east under the down, cut square, with rabbit-runs through its floor. East is Tallow Barrow, which the Tollmere diggers opened in 1012 and which was found walled up again from the inside in the morning. This spring the wall has a gap in it the shape of a door, and the chalk round the gap is warm.

objectives.text: Go to Tallow Barrow
Put down what comes out of the gap after dark
Find what lies at the foot of the gap

stages.journal: A ferret's collar-bell, packed with chalk and warm, at the foot of the door-shaped gap, and the rabbit-runs going in past it and none coming out. The warrener went in on his own feet, after something he heard ring. Tor Rookwright keeps the peace of Rookdown, and the down is part of it.

objectives.text: Tell Tor Rookwright what is done about the gap

options.text: Wall the gap up again, from this side.
Leave it. He went in on his own feet.
Take his ferrets down to Tamwick, so the down has a warrener again.

stages.journal: The rabbits are back on Bram Down, all of them, and the ferrets go down every burrow but one, and the knappers say the deep shaft rings less.

name: One to Dunn
summary: The Hare and Hurdle's chalk board of who owes whom a drink has one debt on it that will not rub off, in the old keeper's hand: One to Dunn, from the Hare. Nobody on the downs knows a Dunn. The house owes a man a drink and the man is nowhere.
notes: The Hare and Hurdle's work. Links the inn, Hound Watch (its keepers drink at the Hare, and its keeper-roll has a name scraped off) and the Last Look.

stages.journal: Top left of the board: One to Dunn, from the Hare, in Cal Merriweather's aunt's chalk. It will not rub off; Cal has tried water, vinegar and a Sayer. The Roll has no Dunn and Pellam Ashcombe does not know a Dunn, and Pellam knows everybody who ever owed anybody. The Wardens who keep the border towers drink at the Hare when they come off their nine days, and the tower nearest the inn is Hound Watch.

objectives.text: Ask at Hound Watch, whose keepers drink at the Hare
Read the tower's keeper-roll

stages.journal: Dunnet Hale kept Hound Watch nine years and a winter, rang the bell at the colossi one night, and went down to see why, and the Rest took his name off the board so the next keeper would not think it was a thing a keeper does. The present keeper has started ringing at the colossi too. Pilgrims leaving the Vale stop at the Last Look for their last sight of green ground; it is the way down from the Hound.

objectives.text: Walk down to the Last Look
Take up what stands in the lee of the stone

stages.journal: In the lee of the Last Look, facing the Choir, a pewter cup with the Hare's mark under the lip, full of clean rainwater, with a grey ring round its foot. The Hare does not let its cups leave the house. Somebody carried one down here a long time ago and it has been kept filled. The debt on the board is the house's, and Cal Merriweather is the house.

objectives.text: Tell Cal Merriweather how the Hare pays its debt

options.text: Pour him the drink at the Last Look, facing the Choir, and bring the cup home.
Write Dunnet Hale under the debt, so the Hare remembers who it owes.
Tell the Wardens their scraped keeper is still owed a drink.

stages.journal: The board at the Hare and Hurdle has been wiped for the Long Table as it is every year, and the skittle alley levelled, and the chalk is honest.

name: Tamwick Twice
summary: Hob Tamwick turns the only cider press in Wickmere nineteen turns a pressing, one for each hearth on Tamwick's line of the Wardens' Roll. The robbers who opened Orm's Long Barrow left a roll in the cist older than the Wardens' own, and Tamwick is on it twice.
notes: Tamwick's work (Hob's dialogue in lake_and_vale.json). Links Tamwick, Orm's Long Barrow and the Singing Yew.

stages.journal: Hob Tamwick counts nineteen turns to a pressing, one for each hearth on Tamwick's line of the Roll, and starts again from one if he loses his place. The shepherds on Bram Down have been talking about the roll the robbers left in Orm's Long Barrow, which is older than Hollin Barrow, older than the Wardens: they say Tamwick is on it twice. Hob would like to see it before he counts another pressing. The hedge-wights stand up among the stones at dusk.

objectives.text: Go to Orm's Long Barrow
Put down the hedge-wights that stand up among the capstones
Take up the roll the robbers left in the cist

stages.journal: The roll is burnt into hide, not inked, one line a hearth, and the Vale's names on it are nearly the Vale's names. Read Tamwick's lines. The second one says where it is.

objectives.text: Read Tamwick's two lines in the roll
Find the second Tamwick where the roll puts it

stages.journal: Tamwick at the yew: one hearth, and a bell in the sapling so it will be found. The Singing Yew is three hundred years of tree grown round a child's bell, humming in any wind, and the hedge-wights will not pass it. A hearth that is one is still a hearth, the roll says, say it with the others or it will not stay. Hob Tamwick counts nineteen.

objectives.text: Tell Hob Tamwick how many turns a pressing takes

options.text: Twenty. Say the yew with the others.
Give the roll to the Wardens and let the Rest decide what Tamwick's line is.
Put the roll back in the cist. It is the barrow's to keep.

stages.journal: Hob Tamwick pressed the first of the autumn's apples at the only press in Wickmere and counted aloud, and Tamwick came to listen, which it does not usually do.

name: Ashcombe on the Roll
summary: Ashcombe emptied in the Ash Winter and is not on the Wardens' Roll, because the Wardens found it on an old tithe list and have not dared to put it back. Pellam Ashcombe carries its name. To put a village on the Roll you need a name for each house, and Ashcombe's front doors are the wall of the Order's West Walk.
notes: Merrowby's work across the grey border. Links Merrowby, the West Walk (walled with Ashcombe's doors; Merrit Ash keeps it) and Ashcombe itself.

stages.journal: Pellam Ashcombe has kept the Wardens' Roll for forty years and says the quiet villages' names to the Toll every dawn so they will not go. He has never said Ashcombe's, because it is not on the Roll, and it is not on the Roll because nobody could say who lived there. His grandmother's grandmother did. To put a village on the Roll you need a name for every house, and the Order walled its West Walk with Ashcombe's front doors, which is where Vale folk used to cut their names.

objectives.text: Go to the West Walk, walled with Ashcombe's doors
Ask Merrit Ash to read you the names on the doors

stages.journal: Merrit Ash has slept behind those doors eleven years and knows every lintel-name by heart: nineteen houses, nineteen names, from Ashcombe-Mill to the Widow's End. Ashcombe's chimneys still draw, though no fire has been lit in them for a hundred and seventy-seven years, and the ash-wights come to the hearths after dark. A house goes on the Roll from its hearth.

objectives.text: Go to Ashcombe
Clear the hearths after dark

stages.journal: Nineteen chimneys drawing on nothing, nineteen hearths cleared, and nineteen names from the doors of the West Walk. Pellam Ashcombe can put Ashcombe on the Roll, or not; the Order has kept Ashcombe in its own way for a hundred and seventy-seven years, in its wall.

objectives.text: Tell Pellam Ashcombe what becomes of Ashcombe

options.text: Put Ashcombe on the Roll, house by house, and say it at the rim at dawn.
Leave it to the Order. Their wall has kept it longer than any roll.
Bring one door home for the Roll room, and let the rest stand.

stages.journal: Pellam Ashcombe went up to the rim at dawn as he always does and said the quiet villages' names to the Toll, and then stood a while longer than usual, and then came down.

name: The Third Arch
summary: Merrowhithe smokes the Mere's pike in the arches of a Builders' aqueduct that has been dry for eleven hundred years. This spring the third arch drips, cold, tasting of stone, and there is nothing up the line of it but the Rudd Cliffs and Skerrow and snow.
notes: Merrowhithe's work, across the border into the Lower Dales. Links Merrowhithe, the Standing Arches, the Stair Bridge, the Rust Scar in Ruddale and Ruddow, whose children were named for the day the Rust Scar ran clear.

stages.journal: The Builders ran the aqueduct down off the heights to somewhere and it broke before the Toll fell; the arches draw like a chimney, which is the only water-work it has ever done for Merrowhithe. This spring the third arch drips onto the landing day and night. Berrit Smoker has not been further up the line of it than the cliff-top, and does not intend to, and would like to know what his fish are hanging under.

objectives.text: Follow the aqueduct up onto the cliff-top, to the Standing Arches
Follow its line down to the Stair Bridge over Rudd Beck

stages.journal: The channel along the top of the Standing Arches is wet from end to end, and the Stair Bridge over Rudd Beck is built of the steps of a Builders' stair somebody took apart: a Merrowhithe mason says the stair went up to the aqueduct's head. The line of it goes up Ruddale into the clans' country. Rudd wash their dead's hands in the rust-coloured water that comes out of the Rust Scar. Clear water is coming down an aqueduct from that side of the fell.

objectives.text: Go up Ruddale to the Rust Scar

stages.journal: Behind the Rust Scar a Builders' channel runs into the rock, dry for a thousand years and wet now, and the scar itself runs as red as it ever did. Ruddow's memory-keeper will know what changed, because she keeps what Rudd remembers, and Rudd remember everything that is owed.

objectives.text: Ask Ushra ko-Rudd at Ruddow what happened at the Rust Scar

stages.journal: One day this spring the Rust Scar ran clear, and every Rudd child born that day was named for it, and the next day it ran red again. Ushra says the fell stopped bleeding for a day. The clear water went down the Builders' channel, and it has been going down it since, a little every day: Merrowhithe's pike are hanging under the water the Rudd clan name their children for.

objectives.text: Tell Berrit Smoker what to do about the third arch

options.text: Catch the drip in a cask and send it up to Ruddow for their namings.
Let it drip. The arches have water in them after eleven hundred years.
Pack the third arch with clay. A smokehouse wants dry arches.

stages.journal: Berrit Smoker has hung the week's pike in the arches as he has for thirty-two years, and has moved the rack from under the third one, and has not said why, and the smokehouse lads have not asked.

name: The Ruled Line
summary: Sedgehithe's reed fringe is going back in a straight line, as if somebody had laid a rule across the bay, a pole's length a week toward the Eelweir. The reedfolk say the Tide account come true; the Sayers say a measurement error; the reeds say nothing.
notes: Sedgehithe's work. Links Sedgehithe, the Heronry, the Eelweir and the Sedge Hearth's peat island.

stages.journal: Everything west of the line has decided it is not reed any more, and the line moves a pole's length a week toward the Eelweir. The herons that have held the dead tower in the wet meadows longer than anyone has held anything on the Mere left all at once this spring, in the middle of the nesting, and flew west. From the top of the Heronry you can see the whole bay.

objectives.text: Climb the Heronry and look at the line from above

stages.journal: From the Heronry the line is plain: a straight brown edge through the green, from the Sedgehithe bollards to the Eelweir, where the Mere goes out west. Reedfolk and Lakefolk share the weir by an agreement neither has read, and leech-hounds come up the channel at night.

objectives.text: Go out along the Eelweir
Put down the leech-hounds that come up the outflow at night

stages.journal: The water through the Eelweir is running harder than the eel-trappers have ever seen it, out of the Mere and down to the Delta, and the traps are full of eels trying to swim back. Somebody has been living on the Sedge Hearth's peat island in the reeds and has taken up the plank from the island side.

objectives.text: Wade out to the Sedge Hearth
Read what was left under the stone on the island

stages.journal: A junior Sayer, measuring the water against the Sedge Hearth's stone every dawn for a month, twelve times: the Mere is falling, and where it falls there is a kerb of Builders' stone a hand under the silt, straight as a rule, from the bollards to the weir. Reed will not root on it. The Circle has told the Sayer it is a measurement error. Maudie Punt cuts the city's thatch off this bay and speaks for Sedgehithe.

objectives.text: Tell Maudie Punt what the ruled line is, and who should hear it

options.text: Tell the reedfolk at the weir: the water is going out, as the Tide account says.
Take the level-book to the Spire. It is not an error.
Cut the reed back to the line and sell it before it browns.

stages.journal: Maudie Punt has tied her punt to the bollard nearest the line, and it hums while it rocks, and she says her mother would have said that was the lake saying the boat's name.

name: The Same Hand
summary: Once a week an entry appears in the toll-ledger at the Stride's Foot: a traveller on foot, going out along the Long Stride to the city, weight of pack given, name given, always in the same large careful hand, and nobody of that name ever comes back through the Foot or is written going in at the city end.
notes: Stride's Foot's work, across the Mere. Links the Stride's Foot, the Larkmouth Bridge (a man sits on its bench until dawn) and Tollmere.

stages.journal: Corin Stilyard has weighed every cart into Tollmere for nineteen years, and his ledger is correct. One entry a week is not his: nineteen since winter, in a hand like a child copying letters. The page is blank when he closes the book and written when he opens it. Somebody sits on the bench at the Larkmouth Bridge every night until dawn, and the Vale's old men will only say that he is waiting for the city's lamps to go out.

objectives.text: Sit with the man on the Larkmouth bench

stages.journal: He is a carter from Wynstead, Hew Coomb, and he has sat on the bench every night since his daughter walked out along the Stride eleven years ago to take a place in the city and did not come home and did not write. Her name is the ninth in the margin of Corin's page. He says the Stride's lamps light one after another at dusk as if somebody were walking out along it, and they go out again one after another at dawn, walking back, and it is only ever one lamp's worth of somebody. The Tallymen at Lantern Row keep the city's rent-rolls.

objectives.text: Ask Orrin Quill at Lantern Row whether the nineteen are in the city

stages.journal: Orrin Quill priced the question, answered it, and showed you the figure: eleven of the nineteen are on the city's rent-rolls, alive, paying, never gone home; eight died in the city and are on the harbour roll. Every one of them went out along the Stride and was never said again in the place they came from. Nobody knows whose hand writes them down. Corin Stilyard's ledger is correct, and he would like it to stop, or to be paid for it.

objectives.text: Tell Corin Stilyard what is done with the nineteen

options.text: Strike the entries. They are not tolls and the ledger is the Guild's.
Copy the names out and send word to the villages they came from.
Leave the ledger open at night, and let the hand write.

stages.journal: Corin Stilyard weighed eleven carts into Tollmere this morning by the sound of their wheels on the planks and entered them correctly, and left the margin alone.

name: The Stride's Dedication
summary: The last block the Builders cut for the Long Stride hangs half-cut in the face of the Old Quarry in the Lower Wold, and on its hidden face is the causeway's own dedication, never laid. Tollmere does not like to be reminded that its famous Oroth causeway came out of a wood it calls savage. Cassa Binder would like a rubbing.
notes: Tollmere's work, across the Mere into the Briarwold. Links Tollmere, the Old Quarry and the Long Stride, and on one branch Elderhold.

stages.journal: Cassa Binder binds and sells books three doors down from the Spire and has copied out all three sides of the Circle's argument by hand, which is a closer reading than any of the three have given the other two. She has heard from a rafter that the half-cut block in the Old Quarry has writing on its hidden face, and she would like it in a book before the Guild has it recut into a doorstep. Weavers string the cut face.

objectives.text: Cross into the Lower Wold to the Old Quarry
Clear the weavers off the cut face
Take a rubbing of the block's hidden face

stages.journal: Three lines, cut before the block was cut out, as if the words came first and the stone was fitted to them. Cassa's paper takes them white. Read what she has made of them, and then walk the Long Stride and count the lamps.

objectives.text: Read the dedication
Walk the Long Stride and count its lamps

stages.journal: Two hundred and six lamp-posts on the Stride, and the Guild counts two hundred and five because the one at the city end has never lit. Each lamp is one who walked it for the first time, the dedication says; the last stone is not laid. Cassa Binder has the rubbing on her bench, and the Guild would pay a good deal to have it lost, and the Woodfolk whose quarry it is have never been asked anything by Tollmere in their lives.

objectives.text: Tell Cassa Binder what becomes of the rubbing

options.text: Bind it and sell it. Let the city read where its causeway came from.
Sell it to the Guild and let them bury it.
Take it to Elderhold. It is the Wold's stone.

stages.journal: Wenna Holt at Elderhold chooses which trees go down the Wold Water to the city, and nobody has ever argued with her successfully. She will know what the Wold wants done with the Builders' writing on its stone.

objectives.text: Take the rubbing to Wenna Holt at Elderhold

stages.journal: Cassa Binder has cut a fresh sheet of rag paper to the size of the block's face and laid it on the bench with nothing on it, and when asked what it is for she says it is for the last line, when somebody lays the stone.

name: The Charter Pins
summary: The Charter of 712 freed the North Road of toll above the Narrows and of blood-price below them, and was cut on a stone the clans broke and the Tallymen mended with brass pins. The pins are being drawn out one a night and there are two left; the Counting Tower's ledger is being kept by someone else, in Oroth numerals.
notes: Tollmere's work on the north shore. Links Tollmere, the Charter Stone and the Counting Tower.

stages.journal: Orrin Quill posts every price the city charges at first light in a hand large enough to read from the bridge, and he does not adjust it for charm. If the Charter Stone breaks the North Road goes back to tolls above the Narrows and blood-price below, and the Guild would make a great deal of money, and Quill says the Guild would also make a great many widows, and that he has priced both. Somebody draws a pin out of the Charter Stone every night.

objectives.text: Go out to the Charter Stone
Wait at the stone after dark for whoever draws the pins
Take up what the pin-drawer was carrying

stages.journal: A dropout Sayer of the kind that signals the Undercroft from North Cliff, with four brass pins in a bag and a chart of the North Road marked with the carts the Counting Tower counts. On the way the North Road crosses the Narrows Bridge, whose clan mark and guild mark were both chiselled off in the same night this spring. The tower has had a clerk counting carts for a tax nobody has paid since 942, and the tower's ledger is being kept by somebody else.

objectives.text: Look at the Narrows Bridge on the way, where both marks were chiselled off
Go to the Counting Tower
Read what is being written in the tower's ledger

stages.journal: The tower counts the North Road's carts in the Builders' numerals against a column the Circle renders as owed back, and the clerk sits at the window and lets it. The Sayer was drawing the pins to break the Charter, so that the road would be tolled again and whatever keeps the tally would have its figure. Orrin Quill has four pins on his desk and a charter-board to post in the morning.

objectives.text: Tell Orrin Quill what is done with the Charter

options.text: Pin the stone again. Both sides still come there to swear.
Let it break. The Guild can toll the road and price the widows.
Leave it on two pins. A charter held by two pins is still a charter.

stages.journal: Orrin Quill posted the board at first light, and on it, in a hand large enough to read from the bridge, is a new line under the North Road's tolls, with a figure beside it, and the figure is what it cost you to walk out there.

name: Cut From Below
summary: Every spring Gullhithe goes over the Gull Cliffs on ropes for the gulls' eggs, and every spring somebody's rope is found cut. This year the cut rope was cut from below. Down at the Pilgrim Stair a Sayer's rope is tied to the last dry step and is still taut, and the stair goes down to the Sunken Barge.
notes: Gullhithe's work under the water. Links Gullhithe, the Eggers' Camp, the Pilgrim Stair and the Sunken Barge.

stages.journal: Jory Wick fishes eels off Gullhithe and says forty marks every morning when he pushes off, and he goes over the Gull Cliffs for eggs every spring with everybody else. This spring his cousin Tam went over on a new rope and came up on half of one: cut, clean, from the bottom end, with the cliff face below him and the water below that.

objectives.text: Go to the Eggers' Camp on the Gull Cliffs

stages.journal: The eggers' ropes hang down the cliff almost to the water, and on the cut one the fibres are pulled upward, not down: whatever cut it was below it, in the water, reaching up. Along the shore the Pilgrim Stair walks straight into the lake and keeps going. A Sayer left a rope tied to the last dry step, and it is still taut.

objectives.text: Go down to the Pilgrim Stair and the taut rope

stages.journal: The rope goes down the drowned steps into the dark to the Sunken Barge, where the Mere's serpent was said to nest forty years ago when North Cliff was last lit. Whatever cut Tam's rope went back down to its nest the way it came.

objectives.text: Go down the stair into the Sunken Barge
Put down what nests in the barge
Find what lies in the nest

stages.journal: In the nest, among the bones of a great many fish and a few that are not fish, a Sayer's hooked rope-knife with its handle wound in a Gullhithe egger's knot. Something has been cutting ropes from below, and it has been using a knife to do it, and the knife was given to somebody by somebody in Gullhithe.

objectives.text: Tell Jory Wick what cut the ropes

options.text: Tell Gullhithe it was the serpent, and it is dead.
Show them the knife. Somebody in Gullhithe gave a Sayer an egger's knot.
Keep the knife and say nothing. The eggers go over next spring either way.

stages.journal: Gullhithe will go over the Gull Cliffs again next spring, on new ropes, and Jory Wick says he will go first, and then says forty marks, as if that were part of the same sentence.

name: Knots Round Nothing
summary: Moreva's eel-traps are coming up empty of eels and full of lantern-makers' knots: hanks of indigo rush tied the way Saeva ties a burial lantern so it floats true, round nothing. The lantern-makers say they were tied for lanterns that went out on the water eighty years ago. And last night the Fog Bell stopped.
notes: Moreva's work. Links Moreva, the Fog Bell and Mor'oul, the stilt-village drowned in a flood nobody recorded, whose lanterns are still lit under the water.

stages.journal: Sauve Mor sets a hundred and forty traps on the North Channel and lifts every one before dawn, and this month nine have come up with a knot in them and nothing inside it. The Fog Bell is rung every quarter hour while the fog is down so the eel-boats can find the channel, and the ringer is paid in eels by Moreva and Isseva both. Last night the bell stopped, and the boats came in to find out why, and the ringer is not in the tower.

objectives.text: Go out to the Fog Bell

stages.journal: The ringer has scratched his tally on the tower post as always, a stroke for every quarter hour rung, and under the last stroke one word in reedfolk letters: knots. His boat is gone from the stilts. The North Channel runs past Mor'oul, the stilt-village that went under in a flood no record has, where the drowned stand at their own doors and the lanterns are still lit beneath the water.

objectives.text: Pole up the channel to Mor'oul
Put down the drowned at their doors
Take up the lantern lit on the roof-ridge

stages.journal: The ringer's lantern was on a roof-ridge a hand under the water, lit, and his boat was tied to Mor'oul's last stilt. Mor'oul's own lanterns burn under the water in rows, every one of them tied with a knot, and every knot tied round a lantern; and there are nine lanterns with no knot. Whatever the traps are catching, it is Mor'oul's knots coming loose, eighty years late, and the ringer went after them to tie them back. Sauve Mor puts the first eel of every morning back so the ones under the water know Moreva is still fishing.

objectives.text: Tell Sauve Mor what to do with the nine knots

options.text: Somebody has to ring the Fog Bell. Moreva can ring it until the ringer comes up.
Take the knots to Saeva to be tied on new lanterns and sent out properly.
Put them back in the traps and let the water take them where it likes.

stages.journal: Sauve Mor lifted his hundred and forty traps before dawn, as always, and put the first eel back, as always, and said go and tell them, and this time did not say who.

name: Which Account
summary: The grey moves up the Greyreed a reed-bed a year, and Nauvissa wants to know which of the four accounts is right before it decides whether to move. The Bell says it does not matter, the Candle says talk and stay, the Breath says go north, and the Tide says wait: it goes out and comes back. Ossa Lissa was raised on the Tide.
notes: Nauvissa's work. Links Nauvissa, the South Stilts (the watchman says the grey comes in at night and goes back by day) and the Greyreed Decoy (its nets torn from inside).

stages.journal: When Ossa Lissa was a girl the grey reeds were at the ash's edge, a mile south; now they are at Nauvissa's landing, and next year they are under her floor. The four accounts each tell her to do something different. The watchman at the South Stilts is paid in eels and has not seen the grey move in twenty years, and this spring he says it comes in at night and goes back by day, and nobody believes him.

objectives.text: Go out to the South Stilts
Stand the night at the stilts and meet what comes in with the grey

stages.journal: The watchman is right: after dark the grey comes up the delta like a tide over the flats, and ash-wights come with it to the foot of the stilts, and before dawn it goes back down, and the reeds it covered are green in the morning, a little greyer. Nauvissa keeps the Boardwalk Gate where the Westway goes onto the delta, and its lanterns were found lit at noon with wet footprints on the boards coming out of the delta. Up the Greyreed the decoyman's dog has started leading something up the netted pipes at night, and the nets are torn from inside.

objectives.text: Go to the Boardwalk Gate, lit at noon
Go up to the Greyreed Decoy
Take the torn net off the pipe

stages.journal: Torn from inside, outward, with the ash on the sea side of the tear: whatever the dog led up the pipes at night broke back out and went down again. The grey comes in and goes back like water. Whether that is the Tide account come true, or the grey learning the marsh's ways, Ossa Lissa has asked for somebody to tell her whether waiting is still the same thing it was.

objectives.text: Tell Ossa Lissa which account Nauvissa lives by

options.text: The Tide is right. It comes in and goes back. Wait.
Go north to Nauve's Landing before it stops going back.
Stay, keep the South Stilts manned every night, and talk to the knights who buy your wicks.

stages.journal: Ossa Lissa has lit the fire on Nauvissa's landing with grey reed, which burns slow and makes a sound as it goes, a small voice, like somebody saying a word in the next room, and the whole hamlet came and sat by it and listened.

name: What the Tide Left
summary: The tide came in over Oulea's shell bank for the first time in three hundred years of tides written on the post, and left footprints on the new salt: bare feet, small ones, coming up out of the sea across the pans and going back again. The Salt Isles ships stopped coming forty years ago.
notes: Oulea's work, down the coast into Cinderlea. Links Oulea, the Salt Pans, the Traders' Post and the Builders' Harbour on the Ash Strand.

stages.journal: Meo Sa knows the tide tables for three hundred years by heart and has noticed they are wrong this year. The Tide account says the drowned will walk when the flood comes back; Meo has boiled salt her whole life on the Tide account and would rather it had waited until she was dead. On the Cockle Beds every family's stake was found moved one row toward the sea. Up the flats at the Salt Pans a pan dried to a crust overnight with footprints across it from the sea side and none coming back.

objectives.text: Cross the Cockle Beds, where every stake moved a row toward the sea
Walk up the tideflats to the Salt Pans

stages.journal: The prints at the Salt Pans are the same small bare feet, crossing the crust inland and not coming back, as if whoever made them had somewhere to be. Oulea still puts up one tent for the Salt Isles traders at the Traders' Post every longest day, and this midsummer somebody pinned a trader's chart to a tent-pole there, and there was no boat on the sea.

objectives.text: Go to the Traders' Post
Read the chart pinned to the tent-pole

stages.journal: Every coast on the chart is drawn as bells except Wickmere's, which is drawn as footprints, and a road is cut across the water from the Isles to the Builders' Harbour on the Ash Strand, with a word at the end the Oulea women read as due. The harbour's mooring posts are bells, and the Salt Isles traders would never moor there: they said the bells ring when a ship is coming that has not yet set out.

objectives.text: Go down the coast to the Builders' Harbour on the Ash Strand

stages.journal: The harbour bells rang last night, the scavengers say. On the quay steps, going down into the Grey Sea, there are small bare footprints in the ash, and none coming up. Meo Sa writes the tides on Oulea's post and has written them true for forty years, and this year she does not know what to write.

objectives.text: Tell Meo Sa what Oulea does about what the tide left

options.text: Put up the traders' tent all year, with salt set out, and wait for the ship that is due.
Write this year's tide on the post as it came, footprints and all.
Send the chart to the Spire. The Circle can read the road across the water.

stages.journal: Meo Sa boiled a pan of salt at dawn on the shell bank, as the Sa family always has, and set the first scoop of it aside on a stone facing the sea, which the Sa family has never done.

name: Against the Current
summary: A burial lantern came back up the channel to Saeva against the current, lit, in a weave the Tal family stopped using eighty years ago, with a grey strand of hair in the rush. Somebody made a lantern in Lisse Tal's great-grandmother's way, with her hair, eighty years after she stopped, and sent it home.
notes: Saeva's work. Links Saeva, Saoul (the lantern-pool whose lanterns are relit every night, and none of the reedfolk does it) and the Tide Hearth, where a knot is tied for a name nobody in Sedgemire knows.

stages.journal: Out on the water the lanterns go down the south channel to the sea and come apart on the way, which is the burial. This one came back up, against the current, lit, and fetched up on Saeva's landing at dawn. The weave is Lisse Tal's great-grandmother's. The village that stood at Saoul moved to Saeva a hundred years ago and left its lanterns on the stilts for Sa'oul, who is in the pool, and the lanterns are relit every night.

objectives.text: Pole down to Saoul
Silence the wisps over the pool after dark

stages.journal: When the wisps are gone the lanterns on Saoul's stilts are still lit, and every one of them is new rush in the old Tal weave, with a grey strand twisted in. Somebody here weaves them and lights them and does not go home. At the Tide Hearth on the Outfall's south bank the reedfolk tie a lantern-knot for everyone the water has taken, and somebody has tied one that stays dry in the spray, for a name nobody in Sedgemire knows.

objectives.text: Go to the Tide Hearth on the Outfall

stages.journal: The dry knot is tied in the Tal weave too, and the name worked into it is Ennet, which no reedfolk has ever carried, because it is a Vale name: a carter from Gosford whom Lisse's great-grandmother buried by water eighty years ago when he came down the Greyreed drowned and nameless, and named him herself so he would not go out unsung. She wove his lantern and she went on weaving. Lisse Tal can read a lantern's maker, year and dead from a single twist of its rush, and she has read this one.

objectives.text: Tell Lisse Tal what is done with the lantern that came home

options.text: Send it out again, properly, down the south channel, sung.
Hang it at Saoul with the others. That is where she is keeping them.
Let the Order have it for the chapter-bell. Lanterns and bells are the same thing said twice.

stages.journal: Lisse Tal is weaving in silence, as she always does, and has taken the old twist up again for one lantern a week, and will not say who it is for, and sings in company as she always does, and the songs are the same.

name: The Boat That Moved
summary: A reedfolk boat is never broken up; when it is done it is left on the tideflats at the Eel-Boat Graveyard, and there are three hundred of them, and some of them have moved in the night. Ollo Nauve built one of the boats that moved, and wants it back where he left it.
notes: Nauve's Landing's work (Ollo's dialogue in sedgemire.json). Links Nauve's Landing, the Eel-Boat Graveyard and the Eel Stews, whose high-walled pond was found empty with its sluice shut.

stages.journal: Every boat on the Sedgemire water came off Ollo Nauve's slipway or his father's. The Alle was his, named by his youngest, and carried one plank of the boat before her as every Nauve boat does, so that she would know where the channels are. He left her at the Eel-Boat Graveyard two winters ago, bow to the sea, and this spring she is a hundred yards up the flats with her bow to the land. The reedfolk say the drowned come ashore to count the hulls.

objectives.text: Walk out onto the tideflats to the Eel-Boat Graveyard
Put down the drowned walking among the hulls

stages.journal: The Alle lies bow to the land among thirty other moved hulls, all turned the same way, all dragged the same distance, all with their old planks gone from them but hers: the drowned have been taking the old wood out of the boats. Hers is still in, wet through, and heavier than bog-oak should be.

objectives.text: Take the Alle's old plank out of her before they do
Follow the drag-marks inland to the Eel Stews

stages.journal: The drag-marks from the Graveyard go up the flats to the Eel Stews, where the Landing keeps its eels alive for the city, and stop at the high-walled pond, which was found empty with its sluice shut and its wall wet on the outside. The old planks are stacked inside it like the ribs of a hull: somebody is building a boat in the pond, out of every boat's memory of the channels, and has let the eels go to make room.

objectives.text: Tell Ollo Nauve what becomes of the Alle's plank

options.text: Put the plank back in the Alle and haul her back to where you left her.
Build the plank into a new boat. That is what an old plank is for.
Take it up to the stews and lay it with the others. Let them finish their boat.

stages.journal: Ollo Nauve went down to the slipway at dawn and caulked nothing, and sat on an upturned hull and looked at the water for an hour, which his caulker says is the first hour he has not worked in thirty years.

name: The Slow Reflection
summary: Eelfathom Pool in the delta shows you a few seconds late; Hesk Pool in the dead city does not show you at all. Ismay Ondrael of the Circle says they are the same water, and that something stands in between. She would like the readings taken by somebody who is not a Sayer, so that nobody can say a Sayer wanted them.
notes: Tollmere's work, across the Mere and down into the grey. Links Tollmere, Eelfathom Pool, Hesk Pool and the Peat Hags, which lie on the line between the two pools, where the cutters have dug up a Warden perfectly kept.

stages.journal: Ismay Ondrael holds that something vast breathed the world out and is breathing it in, and that what lies nearest the mouth goes first. Her colleagues say she is wrong in three different ways. Two pools two regions apart behave as if they were one water with something in the middle of it, and she would like a phial of each, filled and sealed by a hand the Circle cannot be accused of guiding.

objectives.text: Go to Eelfathom Pool in the delta
Fill and seal a phial at the pool's edge

stages.journal: The phial shows whatever is behind it a few heartbeats late. Hesk Pool is in the Ashgrid, in the dead city, down a flight of Oroth steps: the Sayers call it the silence-water and pilgrims do not look into it on the way south.

objectives.text: Go down into the grey to Hesk Pool
Fill and seal a phial on the lowest step

stages.journal: Two phials side by side: one shows the world late and one does not show it. Laid on the chart, the line from one pool to the other runs straight through the Peat Hags in the south marsh, where the cutters dig the turves that warm Isseva and half of Tollmere's poorer streets, and where they have dug up a Warden, perfectly kept, with a roll of names in his hand. Leech-hounds come up to the cuttings after dark.

objectives.text: Go to the Peat Hags, on the line between the waters
Keep the leech-hounds off the cutting after dark

stages.journal: He lies in the cutting in a Warden's grey-green, the colours bright as the day they were dyed, a roll of names in his hand, and the peat around him is dry: dry for a stride round him in every direction, in a bog. Hold the Eelfathom phial over him and he shows in it at once, not late. Hold the Hesk phial over him and he shows in that too. The Wardens want him for the Rest and the Order wants him for the Chapter Roll, and Ismay Ondrael wants her readings.

objectives.text: Tell Ismay Ondrael what becomes of the Warden in the peat

options.text: He is a Warden. He goes to the Rest with his roll.
Let the Order read his roll and walk him to the line.
Leave him where he lies, between the waters, and let the Circle measure what he holds.

stages.journal: Ismay Ondrael has written the two phials and the Warden in the peat into her figures in her own hand and signed them, which she has not done in forty-one years, and has sent a copy to each of her colleagues with no covering note.

name: Flowered in the Frost
summary: Elderhold's doorposts are elder, and do not know they have been made into a door, and this spring they flowered in the frost. Wenna Holt has oiled a stone and said so aloud and is waiting for the Standing Moot's opinion, and the lodge would like it without going to ask.
notes: Elderhold's work, down the Wold Water to the Mere. Links Elderhold, the Grey Man (from whose top the Moot's hum is heard with a word in it), the Tally Hearth (forty notches for trees never planted) and the Rafters' Camp.

stages.journal: Every tree that goes down the Wold Water to the rafters is one that asked: that is the whole of the custom and the whole of the argument. Elder does not flower in the frost. The Woodfolk do not go to the Standing Moot to ask it things; they wait for the Wold to say. From the top of the Grey Man tor the Moot's hum can be heard across the Greatwood, and the foresters say this spring it has a word in it.

objectives.text: Climb the Grey Man and listen for the Moot

stages.journal: The word in the hum is not a word you can say back; it is the sound a stool makes when it is cut out of season. At the forest crossing the Woodfolk hang tally-sticks on the Tally Hearth, a notch for every tree taken, and every notch is a tree planted by the next spring.

objectives.text: Go to the Tally Hearth and count the notches

stages.journal: Forty more notches than new trees this spring. Somebody has cut forty trees that did not ask and notched them on the Wold's own ledger, so that they would look like trees that did. The trees that go to the city go down the Wold Water past the Log Boom, where a raft was let go this spring with nobody on it and went up the river, not down, to the Rafters' Camp at its mouth.

objectives.text: Cross the Log Boom, where a raft went up the Wold Water and not down
Go down the Wold Water to the Rafters' Camp
Deal with the men who brought the forty down
Cut the axe-mark off one of the forty

stages.journal: Two poachers from the Hunters' Stand crew, selling the rafters forty trunks marked with Elderhold's axe-mark, cut with a saw; the rafters paid by the girth and did not look at the mark, and a forester who did was sent down the river tied to a raft. The elder flowered because forty trees were taken that had not finished. Wenna Holt has never been argued with successfully, and custom is hers to keep.

objectives.text: Tell Wenna Holt what the Wold does about the forty

options.text: Plant forty, this autumn, with the whole lodge, and cut forty notches off the sticks.
Do it the Wold's way: the rafters are sold no rope, and nothing is said to their faces.
Take the Guild's price for the forty and plant with it.

stages.journal: The elder doorposts at Elderhold have dropped their flowers, and the lodge is a little taller at the door than at the back, as it is every year.

name: The Fennick Stool
summary: Every stool at Hazelwick has come back after cutting for seven hundred years, and the Fennick stool, cut last winter as the book said, has put up nothing. The Fennicks are a Vale family, in the coppice-book since before there was a Vale, and the last of them walked south this spring.
notes: Hazelwick's work. Links Hazelwick, the Rod Stacks on the Wold's edge, where the last Fennick rods are drying, and Mossgrave, where one moss has been let go that somebody still remembers.

stages.journal: Aggie Coppice keeps the book of which family cuts which stool in which year, and has settled every quarrel over hazel in the Lower Wold for twenty-six years by reading the book aloud until everybody gives up. The Fennick stool is a stump and a stump only. Old Aud Fennick walked south this spring, Aggie hears, and she has not said so to the stool. The last rods cut off it are drying at the Rod Stacks, where the Vale buys its hazel.

objectives.text: Go to the Rod Stacks
Find the last Fennick rods among the stacks

stages.journal: Seven years' rods, chalked FEN on the tie, and every one of them has put out a root at the cut end where it lay on the damp ground: the stool has not died, it has gone into its rods. The Woodfolk bury under named moss and tend the moss until nobody remembers the name, and then let it go, and this spring one moss at Mossgrave was let go that somebody still remembers.

objectives.text: Go to Mossgrave, where the Woodfolk bury under moss

stages.journal: The moss let go was a Fennick's: Wil Fennick, who married into the Wold sixty years ago and was buried under a moss the Woodfolk tended until nobody in the Wold could say his name; they let it go the week Aud walked south. The Warden that stands among the mounds lets you look and does not move. Somebody remembers him: the stool, which has put everything it had into seven years of rods lying at the Rod Stacks with their roots out. Aggie Coppice keeps the book.

objectives.text: Tell Aggie Coppice what the book says about the Fennick stool now

options.text: Keep it in the book as the Fennick stool, cut or not, as long as there is a book.
Plant the rooted rods round the stump as sets. The Fennick stool can come back from them.
Let it go like a moss, and give the stool to a Wold family.

stages.journal: Aggie Coppice read the book aloud at the stools, the whole of it, from the first year, as she does when she means to settle something, and nobody gave up, and nobody argued either.

name: The Listeners' Trunk
summary: The Circle's Listeners left a trunk at Ormhold in 1038 when they came back through the northern gate with salt in their boots, and never came back for it. Nessa Ashby has not opened it. This spring it smells of the sea, and there is no sea north of the Wold.
notes: Ormhold's work. Links Ormhold, Harrow Tor (the road to the northern gate is clear every morning, with no keepers) and the Northgate Stone.

stages.journal: Nessa Ashby guided two Listeners and a chart-maker to the northern gate in 1038, waited three days at the gate stone, and saw them come back on the fourth from the far side with salt in their boots and the chart-maker not speaking. They left a trunk. She charges the Circle for the beds every year by letter, and has never opened a reply. The northern gate's keepers carried every stone they cleared off the road up to Harrow Tor, and nobody has cleared the road since the Chain Years; the foresters say it is clear every morning.

objectives.text: Climb Harrow Tor and look at the road to the northern gate

stages.journal: From the cairn on Harrow Tor the road runs east to the northern gate clean as a swept floor, and there are new stones on the cairn, wet, with sand on them, and nobody has climbed the tor. At the Northgate Stone the Circle's chalk mark from 1038 has not washed off in five years of rain.

objectives.text: Go down to the Northgate Stone

stages.journal: On the step of the Northgate Stone there is a line of grey sand, fresh, blown in under the gate from the far side, and it smells of the sea the way the trunk does. Whatever went through with the Listeners has been clearing the road for them to come back. Nessa Ashby has not opened the trunk because the Wold does not go through, and does not open what it is given to keep.

objectives.text: Tell Nessa Ashby what becomes of the Listeners' trunk

options.text: Open it. Whatever is in it has waited long enough to be read.
Send it to the Spire unopened, with this year's bill for the beds.
Carry it to the Northgate Stone and leave it on the step, for whoever clears the road.

stages.journal: Nessa Ashby has written to the Circle for the beds, as she does every year, and this year she has added one line at the bottom of the bill, and has not told anybody what it says.

name: Opened From the Far Side
summary: The Old Gate's doors were found open at dawn, the bar lifted from the far side and laid on the ground on this side, neatly. The youngest keeper was asleep against them, as she should have been, and woke up on the other side. She came back through and closed it and has not spoken since. Edda Thornby would like somebody to go and look at the far side. Not through. Look.
notes: Rookhold's work. Links Rookhold, the Old Gate Stone, the Verderer's Tower (whose keeper saw a fire beyond the Thornmarch and has not come down) and Countwatch (the count went down by one: the patch moved).

stages.journal: Edda Thornby has kept the Old Gate for forty-four years and slept against its doors for eleven, and holds that a gate is a promise. The keepers of Rookhold swear their oath at the Old Gate Stone with their backs to the gate, so that the last thing they see before they take the watch is the Wold. The youngest swore hers facing the gate. Since the doors were opened, things come to the Gate Stone at night.

objectives.text: Go to the Old Gate Stone
Stand the night at the Gate Stone

stages.journal: Ash-wights, a long way from Cinderlea, come up to the Gate Stone after dark and stand facing the gate as if they had sworn at it. You cannot see the far side from the ground. The Woodfolk's only watch on the east is the Verderer's Tower, built round a living trunk high over the canopy, and the verderer saw a fire on the far side of the Thornmarch and has not come down since.

objectives.text: Climb the Verderer's Tower and look over the Thornmarch

stages.journal: From the top of the tower, past the thorn: a fire, small, at the far side of the Old Gate, where no road is, and going north along the thorn from it in the dark, nine lights, evenly spaced, slow. The verderer will not come down while they are there. Fernhold's foresters chalk the grey patches in the Briar on Countwatch every morning.

objectives.text: Go to Countwatch and read the tally

stages.journal: Nineteen grey patches yesterday and eighteen this morning, and the patch that went off the count did not heal: it moved, along the thorn, to the Old Gate, and stands in the Briar on the far side of it now, the size of a door. Edda Thornby keeps the Old Gate, and a gate is a promise that something will be let through and something will not.

objectives.text: Tell Edda Thornby how the Old Gate is kept now

options.text: Sleep against it yourself, facing the Wold, the way it was always kept.
Leave the bar lying where they laid it. A promise can be kept from both sides.
Send word to Alder Wyke at Fernhold. The patch has moved to your gate.

stages.journal: Edda Thornby has taken the night watch at the Old Gate, as she did for eleven years, and the youngest keeper sat up with her the first night and said one word, and Edda has not said what it was.

name: The Restrung Bow
summary: When a woodfolk hunter dies their bow is unstrung and hung on Hollin Tor, and there are a thousand, and none has ever been restrung. One has. Six Ormhold hunters' bows are missing from the thousand, and the Wold counts them as hung. Edric Fletcher can tell whose hand a bow was made for from the wear on its grip.
notes: Grandfather Hollow's work. Links Grandfather Hollow, Hollin Tor, the Silked Camp and Weaverdeep's larder, and on one branch Ormhold.

stages.journal: Edric Fletcher made every bow in Fernhold and the Hollow but Alder Wyke's, and shoots one arrow a day at the same knot on the same root and has never fetched one. He believes a bow is the only honest tool, because it cannot be used without meaning to. The foresters say one of the bows on Hollin Tor has been restrung, and nobody in the Wold restrings the dead's bows, and Edric would like to see it before anybody touches it.

objectives.text: Climb Hollin Tor
Take down the one bow that is strung

stages.journal: The only strung bow among a thousand, and the string is grey silk that hums. Take it to the man who can read a grip.

objectives.text: Bring the bow to Edric Fletcher

stages.journal: Cobb Ashby's bow: Edric made it for him, and knows the grip, and Cobb was one of the six from Ormhold who slept at the Silked Camp eleven years ago and were not found, and his bow was never hung. The weavers kept the camp as a larder and the Woodfolk left it as a warning. Its back door is Weaverdeep, where the silk bridges hum over the root chasms.

objectives.text: Go to the Silked Camp
Go down into Weaverdeep
Cut a way through the weavers to the larder
Find the hunters' bows in the larder

stages.journal: Five bows in the larder, strung with the same grey silk, humming, laid in a row with their grips toward the way out. Whatever strings them strings them for hands. Edric Fletcher believes a bow does nothing until somebody has chosen a thing and looked at it long enough to know what it is.

objectives.text: Tell Edric Fletcher what becomes of the six bows

options.text: Cut the silk, unstring them all, and hang them on Hollin Tor with the thousand.
They are Ormhold's. Take them to Nessa Ashby; Cobb was her brother.
Burn them, silk and all, at the Silked Camp.

stages.journal: Nessa Ashby keeps Ormhold and charges the Circle for its beds, and she has told nobody but the Listeners' trunk about her brother.

objectives.text: Take the bows to Nessa Ashby at Ormhold

stages.journal: Edric Fletcher shot his one arrow at the knot on the root this morning and then, for the first time in forty years, went and fetched it.

name: The Two Hundred and Seventh
summary: There are two hundred and six lights in the knots of the Grandfather, one for each hearth that has ever been lit in the Hollow, and Pip Hollin counts them from the high walk every night and is never wrong. For three nights she has counted two hundred and seven.
notes: Grandfather Hollow's work. Links the Hollow, the Grandfather's high walk, Barkbridge (a poacher sleeps under its roof every night, and the custom lets him) and the Oiled Stone.

stages.journal: Cille Tamwood oils things: the ropes, the hinges, and the lights when the tallow goes thin. Every light in the tree is the one coal the women carried in from Fernhold, lit knot from knot, and a knot is lit for every hearth ever lit in the Hollow, sat at or not. Pip counted two hundred and seven three nights running. Cille has not been up to look, because if Pip is right a hearth has been lit in the Hollow that nobody has told her about.

objectives.text: Climb the rope walks to the Grandfather's high knots

stages.journal: High in the north wall, in a knot that has never held a light, a small flame lit from the one beside it, which is how every light in the tree is lit and which nobody did. A new hearth, then, somewhere the Hollow counts as its own. Barkbridge's covered spans are the Hollow's too, and a poacher sleeps under its roof every night and nobody moves him on, because the custom says shelter is simply there, and he is counting on it.

objectives.text: Go to Barkbridge and see where the poacher sleeps

stages.journal: He has made a hearth under the middle span: a ring of stones, a fire kept small, a pot, and a bed of bracken, and he is not there. He has been gone every evening, the rafters crossing the bridge say, up the path to the Oiled Stone. The Woodfolk oil their Hearthstone every week until it shines like a chestnut; the forester who forgets is sent to the Briar for a month.

objectives.text: Follow his path to the Oiled Stone

stages.journal: The Oiled Stone shines as it always does, and there is a second rag on the ledge beside the Hollow's rag, and a poacher's oil-flask: he has been oiling the Hearthstone every evening, the way the custom says a forester should, since he lit his fire under the bridge. He keeps the custom that shelters him. The Grandfather has counted him. Cille Tamwood keeps the lights.

objectives.text: Tell Cille Tamwood what is done about the two hundred and seventh light

options.text: Let it burn. He keeps the custom; the tree has counted his hearth.
Put it out. He takes the Wold's harts, and a light is not for a poacher.
Tell Gil Larkfold to let him the back room at the Knot-Hearth, and keep the light.

stages.journal: Pip Hollin counted from the high walk tonight and came down and told her grandfather the number like a sentry reporting, and Cille Tamwood went up with the oil and did not say anything to either of them.

name: The Ninth Door
summary: Dreughow paints the first verse of the Rope-Song on its doors, a word a day, so that a stranger knows where he is in the song before he is let in. Overnight somebody painted an eighth verse over the first on the ninth door, in no clan's hand: a verse's length and metre, Skerrish words that do not mean anything, or mean something nobody has said in a thousand years.
notes: Dreughow's work. Links Dreughow, the Rope Cairn on Brindle Edge (a rope knotted in a fashion nobody has tied for two hundred years) and Ghorrow, the hold with no clan's mark over its door. It does not say the eighth clan's name: that is the Rope-Song's to say.

stages.journal: Brann ko-Dreugh paints a word a day so that the whole verse is new once a year; his grandfather said a verse painted once is a sign and a verse painted every day is a prayer. Every morning at Kharrow the clans breathe four beats of silence for the missing clan, and somebody has filled them in with paint. Brann has not painted over it and has not read it aloud. At the fells' foot the Skerr Stone's Valish face, chiselled off in 942, has been cut back in overnight, badly, in a hand like a child copying letters. On Brindle Edge the Brindle children's outgrown ropes hang on a cairn, and a rope has been added this spring that no family owns.

objectives.text: Look at the Skerr Stone on the Low Road, recut overnight
Climb to the Rope Cairn on Brindle Edge

stages.journal: The new rope is knotted every arm's length in a hitch nobody on the Edge has tied for two hundred years, and there is paint on it, Dreughow's blue, the kind Brann grinds himself. The clans say Ghorrow is a cave: an eighth hold cut in the cliff with no clan's mark over its door and eight doors inside, seven of them bricked, and the one open door goes down. Stone-thralls keep it.

objectives.text: Go to Ghorrow
Put down the stone-thralls at the open door

stages.journal: Over the one open door in Ghorrow, on the bare lintel where a clan's mark should be, the same verse is painted in the same blue, fresh, the brush-strokes going the wrong way for a right hand, like somebody who has watched a verse painted every day for a very long time and never been taught. Brann ko-Dreugh keeps the doors of Dreughow.

objectives.text: Tell Brann ko-Dreugh what is done with the ninth door

options.text: Paint the first verse back over it. Dreugh sing first.
Leave both verses on the ninth door, the eighth under the first.
Copy it for Dunna ko-Kharrow. A verse is a memory-keeper's business.

stages.journal: Brann ko-Dreugh painted his word this morning on the tenth door, as the round says, and stood a while in front of the ninth, and did not paint anything on it.

name: A Debt With a Nicer Voice
summary: Ghast cut Kharrow's chain in the year of the broken bridge and the Moot forgave them, and Kharrow sings the forgiveness every morning before food. If Ghast mends the bridge the song stops, and a forgotten forgiveness goes back to being a debt, so Ghast climb their ladders. Ghast want the bridge mended and the song stopped; Kharrow want neither.
notes: Ghastfell's work, across the Upper Dales. Links Ghastfell, Ghast's Broken Bridge (a mark on its far anchor that is no clan's), the Red Moor (a new stone, and nobody has died) and Kharrow Hold.

stages.journal: Dagga ko-Ghast keeps the long ladders Ghast climbs in and out of its hold by, and would mend the bridge tomorrow and cross it drunk. The elders say the forgiveness verse is what holds Ghast in the Rope-Song at all, and a clan with no verse is a clan the Breath takes. The cut chain still hangs in the gorge, and the goats cross by it, and the bridge's anchor on the far side has a mark on it that is no clan's. The Dale Watch halfway up asks whoever comes up which side of the Moot they stand on, and its horn was blown at midnight this spring by nobody in the watch-house. Crag-wolves den under the anchor stones.

objectives.text: Go up Ghast Dale past the Dale Watch, whose horn blew at midnight
