Go down to Ghast's Broken Bridge
Clear the crag-wolves from under the anchor stones

stages.journal: The far anchor, reached by the goats' chain, carries a ring with a gap in it, cut deep and old, and under it, cut new, Ghast's mark and Kharrow's side by side. The Red Moor is where Ghast and Kharrow fought in the year of the broken bridge, one leaning stone for each of the dead, and the Rope-Song sings it as a debt, not a victory. A new stone stands there this spring, and nobody has died.

objectives.text: Walk to the Red Moor

stages.journal: The new stone on the Red Moor carries the same two marks, Ghast and Kharrow, and between them the ring with a gap: a stone for the bridge itself, set where the dead are, as if the bridge had been one of them. Kharrow sings the forgiveness; Kharrow's Moot-Speaker says the price when blood has been spilled.

objectives.text: Carry Ghast's question up the chain to Torkh ko-Kharrow

stages.journal: Torkh ko-Kharrow held the speaking-bone and heard it and said: the forgiveness is Kharrow's to sing and the bridge is Ghast's to mend, and neither is the other's business, and the stone on the Red Moor is nobody's, and he would like to know who is setting stones for bridges on his moor. That is Kharrow's answer, which is no answer, which is Kharrow's way. Dagga ko-Ghast is waiting at the top of the fourth ladder.

objectives.text: Tell Dagga ko-Ghast what Ghast does about the bridge

options.text: Mend the bridge. Let the song stop and see whether the forgiveness holds without it.
Keep climbing. The forgiveness is sung every morning, and Ghast is in the song.
Ask Kharrow to sing the forgiveness at Ghastfell too, once, across the gorge.

stages.journal: Dagga ko-Ghast climbed down the long ladders at dusk, as she does, and at the fourth one, where outlanders look down, she stopped and looked down, which she has never once done.

name: Aske's Tune
summary: Aske, nine, walked up the sealed Oskeld road in her sleep in the small hours, past the marker, past the shieling, to the sealed shaft, and sat down there, and was found at dawn humming a tune nobody in Oskelcrag knows. The clan-books say the thing in the shaft is holding a note. Ebba ko-Oskel would like to know whose, and would like it not to be teaching it to children.
notes: Oskelcrag's work. Links Oskelcrag, Oskel Shieling (its fire went out one night and the mine's singing stopped), the Deadground (grass growing in a single line toward the mine) and the Oskel Rake.

stages.journal: Oskel followed the silver into the mountain and the silver ran into bone, and the bone started to sing, and one day what was singing came up the shaft, and Oskel sealed the shaft behind it and the road behind that. Ebba knocks on the marker stone every morning so it knows Oskel is still here and still not coming. At the head of the dale the shieling keeps a peat fire lit all year: for the herders, Oskel say; for the mine, the herders say. It went out one night this spring, and for that night the singing stopped.

objectives.text: Go up the dale to Oskel Shieling

stages.journal: The herders say the fire went out the night Aske walked. She passed the shieling in her sleep and the fire went out behind her, and they relit it at dawn, and the mine started singing again as they blew on the peat. Below the mine the Deadground's spoil has grown nothing in a hundred years, and this spring grass has come up on it in a single line.

objectives.text: Walk the Deadground

stages.journal: The line of grass is a child's stride wide and it runs from the marker stone to the sealed shaft, up the Oskeld road, the way Aske walked, green on the grey. Oskelcrag's lead came out of the Oskel Rake before the singing shaft was found, and the miners left the rake when it began to answer their picks: picks are heard there at night, and every morning another yard of the vein is open.

objectives.text: Go to the Oskel Rake
Put down what works the rake at night

stages.journal: Two stone-thralls working the rake with their hands, and between blows they hum, and it is Aske's tune, or Aske is humming theirs. The thing in the shaft holds a note; the thralls work to it; the fire at the shieling is the only thing Oskel has ever found that stops it for a night. Ebba ko-Oskel runs the lead workings and keeps the rule that nobody goes up the Oskeld road.

objectives.text: Tell Ebba ko-Oskel what Oskelcrag does about Aske's tune

options.text: Keep the shieling fire lit day and night, with a herder beside it always, and knock twice.
Teach Aske Oskel's verse of the Rope-Song, to hum over the tune until it goes.
Send her to Ismay Ondrael at the Spire. She is half Oskel and studies the deep places.

stages.journal: Ebba ko-Oskel knocked on the marker stone this morning as she always does, and Aske knocked beside her, and the two of them stood a while, and Ebba laughed at something and did not say what.

name: Forty Head and a Hearth
summary: In the winter of the long snow Rudd fed Kharrow from its own fold and gave a hearth to a family whose house was under the snow: forty head and a hearth. Three times Rudd has been asked to take payment and three times said it was forgiven. Now Rudd has finally asked for the forty head, through the player as Kharrow's go-between, and the reason is on the roll of their dead.
notes: Ruddow's work, up the chain. Links Ruddow, Kharrow Hold (Kun ko-Rudd, Rudd's fosterling there, and Torkh ko-Kharrow) and the Blood-Price Stones by the North Road, where there is coin in the grooves for a death nobody has reported.

stages.journal: Ushra ko-Rudd keeps the memory of Clan Rudd and the account, which is the same thing said with numbers. A debt is a rope between two clans; pay it and the rope goes slack. Rudd have counted what holds the clans together now the Toll hums, and the rope to Kharrow is the one they would keep, and a debt nobody has spoken of in a hundred years is no rope at all. Rudd sent a fosterling up the chain to Kharrow to say the debt was forgiven, and Kharrow kept him.

objectives.text: Go up the chain to Kharrow Hold and speak to Kun ko-Rudd first

stages.journal: Kun ko-Rudd is nine and wears a bone token cut for a grown man: his father's, who died in the long snow, the second one, not the one in the song. Rudd sent the token up with the boy to show Kharrow that Rudd had nothing left to be owed. Kun's father is on Rudd's roll of the dead. Kharrow's toll-keeper has started standing on Rudd's own bridge in Ruddale, saying nothing, which is how Kharrow says a great deal. By the North Road the clans pay blood-price in public, laid coin in the grooves of three stones, and this month there is coin there for a death nobody has reported.

objectives.text: Cross Ruddale Bridge, where Kharrow's toll-keeper stands saying nothing
Go down to the Blood-Price Stones by the North Road

stages.journal: Forty marks in the grooves, Kharrow coin, laid at night, for one death: the price the Moot set, long ago, for a herder lost bringing another clan's beasts down in the snow. Somebody in Kharrow knows how Kun's father died and has been paying for it where nobody is watching, which is not how blood-price is paid. Torkh ko-Kharrow says the price when blood has been spilled.

objectives.text: Ask Torkh ko-Kharrow who laid the coin

stages.journal: Torkh ko-Kharrow did not deny it. He laid the coin himself, at night, because a price paid in the open would have to be sung, and Kharrow would have to sing that a Rudd died for Kharrow's herd in a snow Kharrow's own verse does not mention. He would rather pay twice in the dark than once in the song. Ushra ko-Rudd keeps Rudd's account.

objectives.text: Tell Ushra ko-Rudd what Rudd asks of Kharrow now

options.text: Take up the coin. The price is paid, whoever paid it and however.
Ask for the forty head in Kharrow's hall, before the Moot, and have it sung.
Ask for the boy. A fosterling is a debt too.

stages.journal: Ushra ko-Rudd sang Rudd's verse of the Rope-Song this morning before food, as she does every morning, and it was one line longer.

name: Nine Lights
summary: Skarl's herders have seen a line of lights moving north along the far side of the Briar, beyond the wall, where there is no road: nine of them, the same nine each time, the same spacing, on three nights this spring. Skarl count; it is the one thing they are known for, apart from the doors.
notes: Skarlow's work, along the Thornmarch's northern end. Links Skarlow, Skarl Shieling, the Briar's End (the bone wall pushed outward, from this side) and the Watcher.

stages.journal: Every Skarl door faces east, because the Skarl verse says the giants went east along a road on the far side of the thorn and will come back along it, and if somebody has been gone a thousand years you should at least be facing the door. Varra ko-Skarl has sat outside her hut at dusk facing east every night of her life and is the only person in Skerrow who admits to having seen the lights. The herders at the high shieling sing the cattle down at dusk.

objectives.text: Go up to Skarl Shieling

stages.journal: The herders say the cattle came down at dusk three nights this spring to a verse nobody sang, and those were the nights of the lights. Where the Thornmarch gives out against the fell the Woodfolk walled the gap with bones and the Skarl clan keeps the wall, and neither will say what from. The wall has been pushed outward in the night, from this side.

objectives.text: Go to the Briar's End
Put down what stands up out of the bone wall after dark

stages.journal: The bones of the wall stood up after dark and walked into the gap they had been pushed out of, as if they were trying to close it from the wrong side. Whatever pushed the wall outward went out, not in. The Skarl say the Watcher died watching the Thornmarch, waiting for something to come through it; his skull has turned in the scree this spring, a hand's breadth south.

objectives.text: Climb the scree to the Watcher
Put down the scree-hag nesting in the skull

stages.journal: From the Watcher's eye, which faces south now, you can see along the far side of the Briar, and at dusk nine lights go north along it, evenly spaced, slow. The skull is not watching the Thornmarch any more. It is watching them go past the rest of Wickmere. Varra ko-Skarl keeps Skarlow's eastward watch.

objectives.text: Tell Varra ko-Skarl what Skarl do about the lights

options.text: Rebuild the bone wall, stronger, and tell the Woodfolk it was pushed from our side.
Face east and count them, every night they come. That is what Skarl do.
Send word down the thorn to Edda Thornby at Rookhold. Her gate opened from the far side.

stages.journal: Varra ko-Skarl sat outside her hut at dusk facing east, as she has every night of her life, and counted, and chalked the count on her door, and it was nine, and she chalked it again under the first, which Skarl never do.

name: Answer It
summary: Brodd ko-Brindle hears the Oskeld shaft singing through three valleys of rock and hums it back at the face before every shift, and chalks where his throat finds the note on the headframe post. The old miners say do not answer it. Brodd says somebody should, and is the only one who has said so aloud.
notes: Brindlecrag's work (Brodd's dialogue in skerrow.json). Links Brindlecrag, Brindle Swallow (drop a bell in and listen for it at Brindlecrag's spring), Old Eld's warm bone door and the Smeltings, whose silver has come out ringing.

stages.journal: Midwinter the chalk line on the post was at Brodd's collar and now it is at his breastbone: the note is going down, not softer but lower. Brindle Beck drops into Brindle Swallow and comes out a day later and colder at Brindlecrag's spring, and the miners say it passes the singing shaft on the way. Brodd has given you his shift-bell to drop in.

objectives.text: Drop Brodd's shift-bell into Brindle Swallow

stages.journal: The bell went down ringing and did not stop ringing until the sound was a mile under the moor. Brodd will listen for it at the spring tomorrow. Old Eld, the first silver working on Brindle Edge, was sealed when the singing started at Oskeld, with a door of bone that is a giant's shoulder-blade, and it is warm, and a stone-thrall walks the working after dark.

objectives.text: Go to Old Eld
Put down the stone-thrall that walks the working

stages.journal: With the thrall down, the bone door at Old Eld is warm to the palm, and through it, faint, a bell is ringing, a mile underground, a day before it should reach the spring: Brodd's bell, going past the working toward Oskeld. The silver from the bottom of the vein is smelted at the Smeltings at night with the doors shut and the pipes playing, and this spring it has come out of the mould with a ring in it.

objectives.text: Go down to the Smeltings
Take a bar of the ringing silver

stages.journal: Struck, the bar hums one low note and goes on humming after it has stopped moving, and it is the note on Brodd's post, at his breastbone, going down. The smelters will not name it. Brodd ko-Brindle is the one who says somebody should answer.

objectives.text: Tell Brodd ko-Brindle how Brindlecrag answers the shaft

options.text: Hang the ringing bar in the second headframe and strike it at every shift, as an answer.
Bury it under a bone lintel, the way Ghalorn buries what the dead have agreed to.
Sell it down the pass. Silver is silver in Tollmere.

stages.journal: Brodd ko-Brindle hummed at the face before the morning shift, as he always does, and chalked the post, and the line is where it was yesterday, for the first time since midwinter.

name: What the Ice Keeps
summary: Dunna ko-Kharrow wants the names on Kharrow's Cairns checked against the Rope-Song, and one of them is not in it. Frostmother's Cradle, under the Wall, holds the shapes of what froze in it.
notes: Kharrow Hold's work (Dunna's dialogue in accounts.json), up to the Wall. Links Kharrow Hold, Kharrow's Cairns, the Finger Shrine and Frostmother's Cradle. It is a Kharrow name, not the eighth verse.

stages.journal: Dunna ko-Kharrow keeps what Kharrow remembers: four hundred lines of the Rope-Song, sung every morning before food. Ushka ko-Kharrow kept the memory forty-one years and lost no name, and sang the names of every Kharrow who died on the mountain at the three cairns above the gorge once a year. Dunna would like the cairns' slate checked against the song, line by line, by somebody whose mouth has no habits.

objectives.text: Climb to Kharrow's Cairns
Read the slate of names at the cairns

stages.journal: Harl ko-Kharrow, who went up the Cradle after the lost herd in the winter of the long snow and was not brought down: on the slate and not in the song, and Ushka's own note beside it says her mouth would not sing it. The Finger Shrine in the sinkhole is carved with Kharrow's memory-songs, a line a year; the clans say you do not go up to the Cradle without having slept a night by the finger first.

objectives.text: Sleep a night at the Finger Shrine

stages.journal: The Finger's carving has every line of Kharrow's verse and a gap in the year of the long snow, smoothed, as if a line had been cut and rubbed out by a thumb. Frostmother's Cradle is under the Wall, where the ice holds the shapes of what froze in it. Crag-wolves den in its mouth.

objectives.text: Go up under the Wall to Frostmother's Cradle
Get past the crag-wolves in the Cradle
Take what the ice is holding in the Cradle

stages.journal: In the deepest ice of the Cradle, the shape of a man with his hand out, and in the hand's shape a token, Kharrow-marked, worn on one edge by a thumb. He went up after the herd and he did not come down, and the song that should have carried him down in words did not, and the ice has held him instead. Dunna ko-Kharrow keeps the song.

objectives.text: Tell Dunna ko-Kharrow what becomes of Harl ko-Kharrow's line

options.text: Sing him into Kharrow's verse, where the thumb rubbed out the line.
Give his token to Rudd. He went up after the herd Rudd fed them from.
Leave the song as Ushka left it. The ice is keeping him.

stages.journal: Dunna ko-Kharrow sang Kharrow's verse of the Rope-Song this morning before food, and the clans breathed their four beats after it as always, and one of them was not quite a breath.

name: Would Anybody Say It
summary: Nella Candlewright made Merrowby's candles for thirty years, put on grey three years ago, walked south, and got as far as the rim. She has waited at the Last Camp ever since, making half-candles for the Order, and she has not been able to find out the one thing she is waiting for: whether anybody would say her name if she stayed. Nobody at the Last Camp says names. It is the rule.
notes: The Last Camp's work, north across the grey border and back. Links the Last Camp, Merrowby (Maud Brambling), Candle Cross (a candle in its north niche since midsummer that does not get shorter) and Greywatch (a name read every night for a month that is on no Chapter Roll); on one branch, the Wellspring.

stages.journal: A whole candle is a night; half is a promise to come back and finish it. Nella has a tent full of half-candles, and the knights burn the other halves in the chapter-house on Candle Night. She will not ask anybody at the camp, because nobody there asks anybody anything, and she will not walk back north to ask, because that would be the answer. Maud Brambling bakes Merrowby's bread and hears Merrowby's news, and nothing in Hearthvale is true until it has passed through her.

objectives.text: Ask Maud Brambling in Merrowby whether anybody says Nella Candlewright's name

stages.journal: Maud said it before you had finished asking, and then said it again, the way the Vale says a name to keep it: Merrowby still sends to the empty candle-stall on market days out of habit, and her name is on every Candle Night list. Maud says the Brow sends a candle to Candle Cross every Candle Night, and there is one in the north niche that has burned since midsummer and got no shorter, and one of the knights reads names at Greywatch every night.

objectives.text: Go to Candle Cross on the Brow
Go to Greywatch on the rim, where the Order reads names

stages.journal: In the north niche at Candle Cross, a half-candle of Nella's making, the wick trimmed half-way as she trims them, lit and not burning down: a promise to come back and finish it. At Greywatch the knight on the rim reads the names of the ones who walked down, and every night for a month she has read one more that is on no Chapter Roll, because the woman is not gone on: she is at the Last Camp making the Order's candles. Nella Candlewright has waited three years for this.

objectives.text: Tell Nella Candlewright who says her name

options.text: Merrowby says it, and the Order says it every night. Stay as long as you like; you are said.
Your candle at the Cross is still burning. Go home and finish it. I will walk with you.
The Order reads you at Greywatch already. You can go on south; you will be read.

stages.journal: Nella has put out the last half-candle in her tent and packed the rest for the chapter-house, and she would like somebody beside her on the walk north, as far as the first clean water.

objectives.text: Tell Nella you are ready to walk
Walk Nella Candlewright north to the Wellspring

stages.journal: The knights have taken Nella's half-candles to the chapter-house as they always do, and the chapter-house is the brightest it has been in a hundred years, they say, and it is the only thing she knows she has done since she sat down, and now it is not the only thing.

name: Ossel's Forge
summary: Ossel, a smith's daughter of Gullhithe, kept the West Walk's forge and its round both, and in the autumn of 1019 she went out to bring in a bell-bearer's clapper and did not come back. The forge has not been lit since. It has been lit, lately: three nights, and somebody is working a bell-bearer's clapper on her anvil.
notes: The West Walk's work. Links the West Walk, the Bell Pit (a buried bell dug up, hung from a dead tree and rung once) and the North Gate (something passes through it at the same hour every night).

stages.journal: Merrit Ash has walked the west round four thousand times, from the White Wood to where the reeds go grey, and sleeps every day behind a wall made of Ashcombe's front doors. He was a lock-maker in Tollmere. The Order uses Ossel's quench trough, and the water in it has been changed every week since 1019. For three nights he has come back from the round to find the forge warm and nobody there.

objectives.text: Take up what is lying on Ossel's anvil

stages.journal: A bell-bearer's clapper, half-shaped, by a hand that strikes hard and slow, and warm. The Order buried every bell it could not hang in the Bell Pit so that nobody would ring a broken one, and bell-bearers dig there at night, and one of the buried bells has been dug up, hung from a dead tree and rung once.

objectives.text: Go to the Bell Pit
Put down the bell-bearers digging in the pit

stages.journal: The dug-up bell hangs from a dead ash by a new rope, and it has no clapper, and the bell-bearers were digging for another. Whoever is working Ossel's anvil is making a clapper for this bell. The dead city's north gate stands alone with no wall either side of it, and something passes through it at the same hour every night, leaving the ash disturbed and no tracks.

objectives.text: Go to the North Gate at the hour the ash is disturbed

stages.journal: At the hour, the ash in the arch of the North Gate lifts and settles as if somebody had walked through carrying something heavy, toward the West Walk, and a smell of quench-water comes with it, and the Order's trough is the only quench-water in Cinderlea. Merrit Ash keeps the west walk, and the ring is wherever you turn round.

objectives.text: Tell Merrit Ash what is done with the clapper

options.text: Finish it cold: quench it in Ossel's trough and hang it on the door-wall, unrung.
Put it back on the anvil and leave the forge laid. Let whoever it is finish it.
Bury it in the Bell Pit with the bells the Order would not have rung.

stages.journal: Merrit Ash walked the west round tonight, four thousand and one, and turned round at the grey reeds, and came back to the forge, and stood by the trough a while, and changed the water, though it was not the day.

name: The Late Delivery
summary: The Ash-Winter carts stand in the yard of a roofless waystation, grain still aboard, horses bones in the traces, and the carter's day-book lists a delivery to Greyfold made after the village had walked south. Nan Greyfold lays the tables every dawn for a meal nobody finished, and she would like to know who took it in.
notes: Greyfold's work (Nan's dialogue in cinderlea.json). Links Greyfold, the Ash-Winter Carts and the Silent Market, where one stall has fresh goods on it every morning: bread, a knife, a child's shoe.

stages.journal: Nan Greyfold came as a pilgrim thirty-one years ago, found the tables laid for a meal nobody finished with the ash an inch deep on the plates, and has laid them fresh every dawn since, and took the village's name because nobody else would carry it. Greyfold's people come and stand at their places at dusk and wave, and she waves back. The pilgrims say the carter's day-book at the Ash-Winter Carts lists a delivery to Greyfold after they walked. Ash-wights sit on the cart-beds.

objectives.text: Go to the Ash-Winter Carts
Clear the ash-wights off the cart-beds
Find the carter's day-book under the lead cart's seat

stages.journal: Tam Oakes of Larkbourne Ford carried Greyfold's order in on his back every Hushday after the road went under the ash, bread and salt and a knife for the Fallows' boy and a shoe for the little one who lost hers in the lane, and put it on the tables, and nobody took it, and the next week it was gone. He stopped writing the date. He stopped going home. The pilgrims will not cross the Silent Market by day, and one stall there has fresh goods on it every morning: bread, a knife, a child's shoe.

objectives.text: Read the carter's day-book
Go to the Silent Market
Keep the square at night

stages.journal: At the edge of the square, on a fused-stone stall, bread still warm, salt in a twist of paper, a boy's knife and a child's shoe, laid out the way a carter lays out an order, and the ash round the stall trodden by one pair of heavy boots going away toward Greyfold and none coming back. Somebody is still walking Greyfold's order in, and has lost the way to the tables. Nan Greyfold keeps the tables.

objectives.text: Tell Nan Greyfold what is done with Greyfold's order

options.text: Carry the order in and set it at the tables, where the carter meant it to go.
Leave it on the stall. The market has kept his trade this long.
Take the day-book to the Rest, so Tam Oakes is on a roll somewhere.

stages.journal: Nan Greyfold laid the tables at dawn and cleared them at dusk, and at dusk they came and stood at their places and waved, and she waved back, and then she stood a while longer at the lane's end, looking toward the market, before she went in and shut the door.

name: The Sealed Barge
summary: The Grey Sea brought in a Tollmere barge to the Ash Strand last week with her cargo sealed and her crew gone, and the strand's scavengers have not broken the seal, because a Tallyman's seal is a Tallyman's seal even on a dead coast. Wat Thatcher, sutler to the pilgrims, would like to know whose cargo it is, because he has a guess, and it is his.
notes: Pilgrim's Ash's work, down to the Ash Strand. Links Pilgrim's Ash, the Driftwood Camp and the Strand Beacon, which is lit every night by nobody anyone has met.

stages.journal: Wat Thatcher wears grey over a purse and is embarrassed about both. He brings the pilgrims' candles and cloth up from Merrowby on Hushdays with the cart, and this winter the Order's winter load was too big for the cart, and he had it sent round by sea from Tollmere, because the Stride's toll is dearer than the sea's, and it did not come. The strand-scavengers at the Driftwood Camp have a Tollmere barge on the sand with her seal unbroken.

objectives.text: Go down to the Driftwood Camp on the Ash Strand
Read the barge's manifest

stages.journal: Wat's winter load, sealed: forty bolts of grey cloth, twelve gross of candles, thirty sacks of ash-cake flour, twenty pots and two hundred small bells for the White Wood. Four lakefolk crew, named, paid half before sailing, to land by night at the strand beacon, which the sutler's man would light. Wat has no man. The Strand Beacon is lit every night by nobody anyone has met.

objectives.text: Sit a night at the Strand Beacon
Meet whoever comes to light the beacon after dark

stages.journal: Two of them, grey to the eyes in barge oilskins, came up the strand at dusk with a coal in a pot and lit the beacon, the way the manifest says the sutler's man would, and went for you when you stood up. Four crew; two came to the beacon; the other two are somewhere on the strand, still bringing the barge in. The load is still sealed. It is Wat's, and the Order's, and it came through the grey to get here.

objectives.text: Tell Wat Thatcher what becomes of the sealed load

options.text: Break the seal. It is the Order's winter; carry it up to Pilgrim's Ash.
Send word to the Guild at Tollmere and let them collect their seal and bill you.
Give it to the strand's scavengers. The sea brought it to them.

stages.journal: Wat Thatcher has cut four notches on the inside of the cart lid, on the bell side, and has not said who for, and Cadwen Ash looked at them for a long time and did not say anything either.
